From the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation to the Euler-Maxwell equation in the semiclassical limit

Immanuel Ben-Porat Address: Immanuel Ben Porat, The University of Texas at Austin, Austin, TX 78712, USA. Email address: immanuel.benporat@austin.utexas.edu
Abstract.

We derive the pressureless Euler-Maxwell system as a semiclassical limit from the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation. The method relies on studying a quantum modulated energy accounting for the self-consistent magnetic effects. Crucially, a correction is incorporated in the quantum modulated energy as to enable to close the Grönwall estimate provided a smallness assumption on the initial data is imposed. This is the first result on the semiclassical limit of the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation avoiding any regularization or conditional uniform in ℏ\hbar bounds on the wave function.

1. Introduction

1.1. Background.

One of the most commonly studied models in non-relativistic quantum mechanics is the Hartree equation

{i​ℏ​∂tψℏ=−ℏ22​Δ​ψℏ+V∗|ψℏ|2​ψℏψℏ​(0,⋅)=ψℏin,\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{lc}\begin{cases}i\hbar\partial_{t}\psi_{\hbar}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2}\Delta\psi_{\hbar}+V\ast\left|\psi_{\hbar}\right|^{2}\psi_{\hbar}\\ \psi_{\hbar}(0,\cdot)=\psi_{\hbar}^{\mathrm{in}},&\end{cases}\end{array}

describing the evolution of a wave function ψℏ\psi_{\hbar} via a self-consistent quantum Hamiltonian given by means of an interaction V:ℝ3→ℝV:\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and scaled via Planck’s constant 0<ℏ≪10<\hbar\ll 1. The problem of identifying the classical dynamics resulting from Hartree’s equation as Planck’s constant ℏ\hbar becomes negligible is a prototypical example of a semiclassical limit. The semiclassical limit is motivated by the fact that the scaling parameter ℏ\hbar measures how quantum the system is, and as it becomes small the system is approximately classical. We refer to [27] for a particularly accessible exposition of the physical background. It turns out that the Vlasov equation is the kinetic PDE that is expected to be derived from (1.1), namely

{∂tf+ξ⋅∇xf−∇V∗ρf⋅∇ξf=0,ρf=∫ℝ3f(t,x,ξ)dξf⁡(0,⋅)=fin.\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{lc}\begin{cases}\partial_{t}f+\xi\cdot\nabla_{x}f-\nabla V\ast\rho_{f}\cdot\nabla_{\xi}f=0,\ \rho_{f}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}f(t,x,\xi)\ {\rm d}\xi\\ f(0,\cdot)=f^{\mathrm{in}}.\end{cases}\end{array}

We do not aim to give an exhaustive account of the literature concerning the rigorous justification of the semiclassical limit leading from (1.1) to (1.1) but refer to the foundational works by Lions-Paul [18] and Markowich-Mauser [20]. Other more modern works on the semiclassical limit include [7, 6, 13, 12, 14, 26]. We refer to Chapter 3 in [19] for a detailed review of quantum optimal transport and its applications in semiclassical and quantum many-body limits. A more realistic (and hence more involved) description of quantum matter includes a quantum Hamiltonian with a self-consistent electromagnetic part, which leads to the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation given by

{iℏ∂tψℏ=12(iℏ∇+Aℏ)2ψℏ+φℏψℏ−Δ​φℏ=ρℏ(∂t​t−Δ)Aℏ=ℙJℏdiv​Aℏ=0\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{lc}\begin{cases}&i\hbar\partial_{t}\psi_{\hbar}=\frac{1}{2}(i\hbar\nabla+A_{\hbar})^{2}\psi_{\hbar}+\varphi_{\hbar}\psi_{\hbar}\\ &-\Delta\varphi_{\hbar}=\rho_{\hbar}\\ &(\partial_{tt}-\Delta)A_{\hbar}=\mathbb{P}J_{\hbar}\\ &\mathrm{div}A_{\hbar}=0\end{cases}\end{array}

supplemented with initial data

(MSin) (ψℏ​(0,⋅),Aℏ​(0,⋅),∂tAℏ​(0,⋅))=(ψℏin,A0,ℏin,A1,ℏin),‖ψℏin‖2=1,div⁡(A0,ℏin)=div⁡(A1,ℏin)=0.\displaystyle(\psi_{\hbar}(0,\cdot),A_{\hbar}(0,\cdot),\partial_{t}A_{\hbar}(0,\cdot))=(\psi^{\mathrm{in}}_{\hbar},A_{0,\hbar}^{\mathrm{in}},A^{\mathrm{in}}_{1,\hbar}),\ \left\|\psi^{\mathrm{in}}_{\hbar}\right\|_{2}=1,\ \mathrm{div}(A_{0,\hbar}^{\mathrm{in}})=\mathrm{div}(A^{\mathrm{in}}_{1,\hbar})=0.

Here we designate by ρℏ,Jℏ\rho_{\hbar},J_{\hbar} the quantum density and quantum current, respectively, defined by

(1.4) Jℏ≔−ℜ(ψℏ¯(iℏ∇+Aℏ)ψℏ),ρℏ≔|ψℏ|2\displaystyle J_{\hbar}\coloneqq-\Re(\overline{\psi_{\hbar}}(i\hbar\nabla+A_{\hbar})\psi_{\hbar}),\ \rho_{\hbar}\coloneqq\left|\psi_{\hbar}\right|^{2}

and we designate by ℙ\mathbb{P} the Helmholtz-Leray projector defined by

(1.5) ℙJ≔(I−∇Δ−1div)J.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}J\coloneqq(I-\nabla\Delta^{-1}\mathrm{div})J.

Note that Aℏ:[0,T]×ℝ3→ℝ3A_{\hbar}:[0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{3}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{3} is to be interpreted as a magnetic vector potential. The expected semiclassical limit in this case is the non-relativistic Vlasov-Maxwell equation

(VM) {∂tf+ξ⋅∇xf+(E+ξ×B)⋅∇ξf=0∂tE−curl​B=−J,Jf=∫ℝ3ξ​f​(t,x,ξ)​𝑑ξ∂tB+curl​E=0divE=ρf,divB=0,ρf=∫ℝ3f(t,x,ξ)dξ.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\begin{array}[]{lc}\partial_{t}f+\xi\cdot\nabla_{x}f+(E+\xi\times B)\cdot\nabla_{\xi}f=0\\ \partial_{t}E-\mathrm{curl}B=-J,\ J_{f}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\xi f(t,x,\xi)\ {\rm d}\xi\\ \partial_{t}B+\mathrm{curl}E=0\\ \mathrm{div}E=\rho_{f},\mathrm{div}B=0,\ \rho_{f}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}f(t,x,\xi)\ {\rm d}\xi.\end{array}\end{cases}

The rigorous derivation leading from (1.1) to (VM) in the limit as ℏ→0\hbar\rightarrow 0 is well recognized as an outstanding open problem. However, there have been several intermediate and related results which we now review. The semiclassical limit for a regularized version of (1.1) and (VM) (a regularization modeling extended charges) has been proved in [16]. The regularization has the clear advantage that it compensates for the loss of derivative which is usually a major source of difficulty in (VM), and results from the fact that E,BE,B are evolve hyperbolically (unlike the electrostatic case demonstrated in (1.1)). In [15] the regularized Maxwell-Schrödinger equation is obtained as a mean-field limit from the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian and in [17] the author goes further to derive the regularized Vlasov-Maxwell equation as a combined mean-field semiclassical limit from quantum many-body dynamics. It is also possible to study the semiclassical limit for monokinetic initial data in the following manner. Introducing the monokinetic ansatz f⁡(t,x,ξ)=ρ⁡(t,x)​δ​(ξ−u⁡(t,x))f(t,x,\xi)=\rho(t,x)\delta(\xi-u(t,x)) a direct calculation reveals that ff is a solution of (VM) iff (ρ,u,B,E)(\rho,u,B,E) is a solution of the following Euler-Maxwell system:

(EM) {∂tρ+div⁡(ρ​u)=0∂tu+u​Dx​u=E+u×B∂tE−curl​B=−ρ​u∂tB+curl​E=0div​E=ρ,div⁡(B)=0\displaystyle\begin{cases}\begin{array}[]{lc}\partial_{t}\rho+\mathrm{div}(\rho u)=0\\ \partial_{t}u+uD_{x}u=E+u\times B\\ \partial_{t}E-\mathrm{curl}B=-\rho u\\ \partial_{t}B+\mathrm{curl}E=0\\ \mathrm{div}E=\rho,\ \mathrm{div}(B)=0\end{array}\end{cases}

supplemented with initial data

(EMin) (ρ⁡(0,⋅),u⁡(0,⋅),B⁡(0,⋅),E⁡(0,⋅))=(ρin,uin,Bin,Ein),ρin∈𝒫⁡(ℝ3),div​Ein=ρin,div​Bin=0.\displaystyle(\rho(0,\cdot),u(0,\cdot),B(0,\cdot),E(0,\cdot))=(\rho^{\mathrm{in}},u^{\mathrm{in}},B^{\mathrm{in}},E^{\mathrm{in}}),\ \rho^{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{3}),\ \mathrm{div}E^{\mathrm{in}}=\rho^{\mathrm{in}},\ \mathrm{div}B^{\mathrm{in}}=0.

In this sense, (EM) may be viewed as a special case of (VM) with initial data ρin​δ​(ξ−uin)\rho^{\mathrm{in}}\delta(\xi-u^{\mathrm{in}}). The derivation of the Euler-Maxwell equation with pressure as a semiclassical limit has been studied in [11] via the modulated energy method, which will be central for the present work as well. Nevertheless, the result in [11] is conditional since it assumes a bound uniform in ℏ\hbar on ψℏ\psi_{\hbar}, i.e. a bound of the form

(1.6) sup0<ℏ≤1​supt∈[0,T]​‖ψℏ​(t,⋅)‖∞<∞.\displaystyle\underset{0<\hbar\leq 1}{\sup}\underset{t\in[0,T]}{\sup}\left\|\psi_{\hbar}(t,\cdot)\right\|_{\infty}<\infty.

Such bounds are not known at present, and in fact even in the simplified electrostatic settings of the Hartree equation (1.1) an estimate of the form (1.6) has been proved in 3​D3D only in the case where VV is the screened Coulomb interaction and the initial data verifies smallness assumptions [14]. The related problem of propagation of quantum velocity moments of arbitrary order uniformly in ℏ\hbar for (1.1) is explicitly classified as an open problem in [9]. However, the pressureless Euler-Poisson equation has already been derived (non-conditionally) as a semiclassical limit in the important work by Golse-Paul [8]. A more recent work which is particularly relevant to the problem at stake is [24], in which the author derives the relativistic Euler-Maxwell equation from the massive Klein–Gordon–Maxwell system (which can be viewed as a relativistic version of (1.1)). Other related works about the semiclassical limit of quantum dynamics coupled to Maxwell type equations include [22], where the authors implement WKB methods to derive the Euler-Poisswell equation from the Pauli–Poisswell equation, and [21], in which the combined non-relativistic semiclassical limit of the Dirac-Maxwell equation is proved. To finish this discussion, we also mention that it is interesting to study the semiclassical limit when the magnetic field is external rather than coupled – this line of research was initiated by Arnold-Steinrück in [2], who employed a Wigner transform approach, and was also undertaken more recently by the author in [4, 5], by exploiting machinery from quantum optimal transport and quantum modulated energies.

1.2. Main results

The main purpose of this work is to prove the semiclassical limit leading from (1.1) to (EM) for small initial data. This demonstrates a first step towards the resolution of the formidable problem mentioned earlier regarding the derivation of (VM) semiclassically from (1.1) – our main result settles this problem for small monokinetic initial data. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result regarding the semiclassical limit of the non-relativistic Maxwell-Schrödinger equation which does not necessitate any regularization or conditional assumptions of the type (1.6). Our underlying methodology rests upon identifying a corrected quantum modulated energy, which we now define. Given a solution (ψℏ,Aℏ,φℏ)(\psi_{\hbar},A_{\hbar},\varphi_{\hbar}) to (1.1) and a solution (ρ,u,B,E)(\rho,u,B,E) to (EM) set Eℏ≔−∂tAℏ−∇φℏE_{\hbar}\coloneqq-\partial_{t}A_{\hbar}-\nabla\varphi_{\hbar}, Bℏ≔curl​AℏB_{\hbar}\coloneqq\mathrm{curl}A_{\hbar} and define the quantum modulated energy by

and the corrected quantum modulated energy by

(1.8) 𝒢ℏ​(t)≔ℋℏ​(t)−∫ℝ3u⋅((Eℏ−E)×(Bℏ−B))​𝑑x.\displaystyle\mathcal{G}_{\hbar}(t)\coloneqq\mathcal{H}_{\hbar}(t)-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}u\cdot((E_{\hbar}-E)\times(B_{\hbar}-B))\ {\rm d}x.

Given a solution ψℏ\psi_{\hbar} to (1.1) we set Rℏ​(t)≔|ψℏ​(t,⋅)⟩|⟨ψℏ​(t,⋅)|R_{\hbar}(t)\coloneqq|\psi_{\hbar}(t,\cdot)\rangle|\langle\psi_{\hbar}(t,\cdot)|. By direct calculation RℏR_{\hbar} is governed by the following equation:

{iℏ∂tRℏ=[12(iℏ∇+Aℏ)2+φℏ,Rℏ]−Δ​φℏ=ρℏ(∂t​t−Δ)Aℏ=ℙJℏ,div​Aℏ=0.\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{lc}\begin{cases}&i\hbar\partial_{t}R_{\hbar}=\left[\frac{1}{2}(i\hbar\nabla+A_{\hbar})^{2}+\varphi_{\hbar},R_{\hbar}\right]\\ &-\Delta\varphi_{\hbar}=\rho_{\hbar}\\ &(\partial_{tt}-\Delta)A_{\hbar}=\mathbb{P}J_{\hbar},\\ &\mathrm{div}A_{\hbar}=0.\end{cases}\end{array}

([23], Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2) Suppose that (ψℏin,A0,ℏin,A1,ℏin)∈H4​(ℝ3)×H4​(ℝ3)×H3​(ℝ3)(\psi^{\mathrm{in}}_{\hbar},A^{\mathrm{in}}_{0,\hbar},A^{\mathrm{in}}_{1,\hbar})\in H^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\times H^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\times H^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) satisfies (MSin). 1.3. Strategy and key ideas.

Prior to establishing the semiclassical limit leading from a dispersive to a monokinetic PDE, one has to first gain a proper understanding of the weak-strong stability exhibited by the underlying monokinetic PDE. To be concrete, given solutions (ρ1,u1,E1,B1)(\rho_{1},u_{1},E_{1},B_{1}) and (ρ2,u2,E2,B2)(\rho_{2},u_{2},E_{2},B_{2}) to (EM) define the modulated energy by

(1.14) ℋ⁡(t)\displaystyle\mathcal{H}(t) ≔12​∫ℝ3ρ1​|u1−u2|2​dx⏟≔𝒰⁡(t)+12​∫ℝ3|E1−E2|2​dx⏟≔ℰ⁡(t)+12​∫ℝ3|B1−B2|2​dx⏟≔ℬ⁡(t)\displaystyle\coloneqq\underset{\coloneqq\mathcal{U}(t)}{\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\rho_{1}\left|u_{1}-u_{2}\right|^{2}\ {\rm d}x}}+\underset{\coloneqq\mathcal{E}(t)}{\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\left|E_{1}-E_{2}\right|^{2}\ {\rm d}x}}+\underset{\coloneqq\mathcal{B}(t)}{\underbrace{\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\left|B_{1}-B_{2}\right|^{2}\ {\rm d}x}}

and the corrected modulated energy by

(1.15) 𝒢⁡(t)≔ℋ⁡(t)−∫ℝ3u2⋅((E1−E2)×(B1−B2))​𝑑x.\displaystyle\mathcal{G}(t)\coloneqq\mathcal{H}(t)-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}u_{2}\cdot((E_{1}-E_{2})\times(B_{1}-B_{2}))\ {\rm d}x.

Note that ℋ⁡(t)\mathcal{H}(t) and 𝒢⁡(t)\mathcal{G}(t) are the classical analogues of (1.7) and (1.8), respectively. A weak-strong stability principle would typically be an evolution estimate of the type

dd​t​(modulated energy)≤C⁡(modulated energy)​with​C=C⁡(‖ρ2‖∞,‖u2‖Wt,x1,∞​([0,T]×ℝ3)).\displaystyle\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}(\mbox{modulated energy})\leq C(\mbox{modulated energy})\ \mbox{with}\ C=C(\left\|\rho_{2}\right\|_{\infty},\left\|u_{2}\right\|_{W^{1,\infty}_{t,x}([0,T]\times\mathbb{R}^{3})}).

Crucially, the constant CC involves only the regularity of one of the solutions. A weak-strong stability inequality is well established for the pressureless Euler-Poisson equation – see appendix A. in [25]. An attempt to mimic the proof of this weak-strong stability inequality would include the calculation of the time derivative of the modulated energy (1.14). This calculation is performed in Theorem 2.4 and results in the following formula

dd​t​ℋ​(t)=\displaystyle\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\mathcal{H}(t)= −∫ℝ3ρ1(u1−u2)⊗2:Dxu2dx−∫ℝ3(ρ1−ρ2)u2⋅(E1−E2)dx\displaystyle-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\rho_{1}(u_{1}-u_{2})^{\otimes 2}:D_{x}u_{2}\ {\rm d}x-\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}(\rho_{1}-\rho_{2})u_{2}\cdot(E_{1}-E_{2})\ {\rm d}x
(1.16) +∫ℝ3ρ1(u1−u2)⋅(u2×(B1−B2))dx.\displaystyle+\int_{\mathbb{R}^{3}}\rho_{1}(u_{1}-u_{2})\cdot(u_{2}\times(B_{1}-B_{2}))\ {\rm d}x.

It is transparent that the first term in the right-hand side of (1.16) can be bounded by means of 𝒰⁡(t)\mathcal{U}(t) up to a constant depending only on the regularity of u2u_{2} – see §2.2 for details. However, the last term in (1.16) would require an L∞L^{\infty} bound on ρ1\rho_{1}, and therefore such a bound would not enable to obtain a weak-strong stability principle. We stress that we wish to avoid at all costs any dependence on the L∞L^{\infty} norm of ρ1\rho_{1}: in the semiclassical limit ρ1\rho_{1} will play the role of ρℏ\rho_{\hbar}, and we already remarked that it is currently not possible to rule out that supt∈[0,T]​‖ρℏ​(t,⋅)‖∞\underset{t\in[0,T]}{\sup}\left\|\rho_{\hbar}(t,\cdot)\right\|_{\infty} blows up as ℏ→0\hbar\rightarrow 0. The idea of the corrected modulated energy (1.15) is to circumvent this issue. Indeed, once the correction is incorporated within the modulated energy it is possible to deduce a weak-strong inequality for small initial data by observing that 𝒢\mathcal{G} is bounded from below and above in terms of ℋ\mathcal{H} as long as u2u_{2} remains small (see Lemma 2.5). More precisely it holds that

(1−Λ)​ℋ​(t)≤𝒢⁡(t)≤(1+Λ)​ℋ​(t)​as long as​‖u2‖∞≤Λ​for some​Λ<1.\displaystyle(1-\Lambda)\mathcal{H}(t)\leq\mathcal{G}(t)\leq(1+\Lambda)\mathcal{H}(t)\ \mbox{as long as}\ \left\|u_{2}\right\|_{\infty}\leq\Lambda\ \mbox{for some}\ \Lambda<1.

The plan outlined above enables to prove a weak-strong stability principle for (EM) under smallness assumptions. Conceptually, this is similar in spirit to the adapted modulated energy implemented in [24], and a major part of the novelty of the present work is that this idea can be imported to the settings of the Maxwell-Schrödinger equation. This component is also the reason the final result is unconditional, in variance with [11]. Having bypassed this issue, the next task is to quantize the weak-strong stability argument, which is where the quantum modulated energies (1.7)-(1.8) come into play.

The paper is organized as follows. In §2 we prove the local well-posedness of (EM). Note that since we are considering the pressureless Euler-Maxwell equation local well-posedness is natural (in variance with [11], which includes a pressure term leading to a global theory). Afterwards, we prove the weak-strong stability principle by studying the evolution of the corrected modulated energy 𝒢⁡(t)\mathcal{G}(t). In §3 we present a proof of the semiclassical limit leading from (1.1) to (EM) as formulated in Theorem 1.2.

2. Local well-posedness and weak-strong stability for (EM)

2.1. Local in time existence of classical solutions to (EM)

We start by demonstrating local in time existence of classical solutions to (EM). The proof differs substantially from the local well-posedness theory of Euler-Poisson due to the fact that EE and BB are governed dynamically according to a hyperbolic equation. The local existence is proved only for small initial data, which is more restrictive than the local existence for the Euler-Poisson equation. The following theorem goes back to the work of Kato [10] and has been revised in [28].

2.2. Weak-strong stability for (EM)

In this section we prove a weak-strong stability inequality for the Euler-Maxwell equation (EM). As mentioned in the introduction, the weak-strong stability principle already captures one key idea which reflects the novelty of this work, namely incorporating a corrector within the modulated energy. The proof of the semiclassical limit in the next section will be modeled on this inequality. The main theorem of this section is stated below.

One may construct admissible initial data, that is initial data such that ℋℏ​(0)​→ℏ→0​0\mathcal{H}_{\hbar}(0)\underset{\hbar\rightarrow 0}{\rightarrow}0. In more detail, for given (ρin,uin,Ein,Bin)(\rho^{\mathrm{in}},u^{\mathrm{in}},E^{\mathrm{in}},B^{\mathrm{in}}) satisfying (EMin) we may find (ψℏin,A0,ℏin,A1,ℏin)(\psi_{\hbar}^{\mathrm{in}},A^{\mathrm{in}}_{0,\hbar},A^{\mathrm{in}}_{1,\hbar}) satisfying (MSin) such that

and

and

We further assume that Bin=curl​A0~B^{\mathrm{in}}=\mathrm{curl}\widetilde{A_{0}} for some A0~∈H5​(ℝ3)\widetilde{A_{0}}\in H^{5}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) with div​A0~=0\mathrm{div}\widetilde{A_{0}}=0. We may then choose A0,ℏin≡A0~A^{\mathrm{in}}_{0,\hbar}\equiv\widetilde{A_{0}} so that ℬℏ​(0)≡0\mathcal{B}_{\hbar}(0)\equiv 0. Moreover assume there exist some A1~∈H4​(ℝ3)\widetilde{A_{1}}\in H^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) with div​A1~=0\mathrm{div}\widetilde{A_{1}}=0 such that Ein=∇Δ−1ρin−A1~E^{\mathrm{in}}=\nabla\Delta^{-1}\rho^{\mathrm{in}}-\widetilde{A_{1}}. So choosing A1,ℏin=A1~A_{1,\hbar}^{\mathrm{in}}=\widetilde{A_{1}} we get

According to Proposition 6.1 in [5], given ρin∈H3​(ℝ3)∩𝒫⁡(ℝ3)\rho^{\mathrm{in}}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}^{3})\cap\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) and uin∈H4​(ℝ3),A0in∈H4​(ℝ3)u^{\mathrm{in}}\in H^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{3}),A^{\mathrm{in}}_{0}\in H^{4}(\mathbb{R}^{3}) there exists a family of wave functions {ψℏin}ℏ>0\{\psi_{\hbar}^{\mathrm{in}}\}_{\hbar>0} such that

ℋℏ​(0)=𝒰ℏ​(0)+ℰℏ​(0)​→ℏ→0​0.\displaystyle\mathcal{H}_{\hbar}(0)=\mathcal{U}_{\hbar}(0)+\mathcal{E}_{\hbar}(0)\underset{\hbar\rightarrow 0}{\rightarrow}0.

Thus (ψℏin,A0~,A1~)(\psi_{\hbar}^{\mathrm{in}},\widetilde{A_{0}},\widetilde{A_{1}}) is the requested initial data.
